analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies and large federal contractors to pay workers at least a poverty-level wage for a family of four.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the federal government and companies holding federal contracts worth more than $10,000 to pay every worker enough that full-time work covers the federal poverty level for a family of four, plus extra pay for fringe benefits the employer doesn't provide. Companies that repeatedly violate the rule could lose their contracts and be barred from federal contracting for five years, and workers could sue for back pay. Small businesses and most smaller nonprofits would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers employed by the federal government and by federal contractors — often janitors, food service workers, security guards, and other low-wage service employees — whose full-time pay currently falls below the poverty line for a family of four. The bill also protects them from being fired for complaining, and gives them the right to sue for unpaid wages, triple damages in willful cases, and attorney fees.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every worker under the bill's coverage to earn, working 40 hours a week, at least the federal poverty level for a family of four, plus a locality-based supplement covering fringe benefits like health insurance, retirement, and paid leave that the employer doesn't provide [S2][S3].
Makes it illegal to fire or suspend a worker for alleging a wage violation, and lets workers sue for back pay, attorney fees, and triple damages when a violation is willful [S3].

Federal contractors with a pattern of violations could have their contracts canceled, be liable for the government's cost of finding a replacement, and be barred from federal contracts for five years [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors and federal agencies, which would bear higher labor costs, likely passed on to taxpayers through contract prices. Contractors also face debarment and replacement-cost liability if they repeatedly violate the wage floor. Small businesses and nonprofits with modest pay ratios are exempt, so the cost falls on larger firms.

drawbacks.text: Higher wages on federal contracts would raise the government's cost of goods and services, a cost ultimately borne by taxpayers; the bill contains no dedicated funding [S3].

The wage floor is defined by the poverty level for a family of four regardless of household size, so it is less targeted than a per-household standard, and the broad definition of 'employer' as anyone with economic power over work terms could reach fissured arrangements like staffing and subcontracting chains [S3].

The exemptions are broad: every small business is exempt, and tax-exempt nonprofits are exempt so long as their CEO earns no more than 25 times their lowest-paid worker, leaving many low-wage workers in the covered sectors unprotected [S2][S3].
The President may suspend the entire act in times of emergency, a broad carve-out an honest supporter would acknowledge as a potential loophole [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a direct, enforceable pay floor for a large, identifiable group of workers whose full-time work does not lift a family out of poverty, with strong enforcement teeth — debarment, restitution, and a private right of action. The real cost is higher contract prices borne by taxpayers and covered contractors, and the design is rough in places: the one-size family-of-four benchmark and the wide exemptions mean some needy workers are missed and some costs are untargeted. On balance it is a straightforward wage transfer from contractors (and indirectly taxpayers) to low-wage federal contract workers, and it was never seriously considered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2009 and referred to two House committees, which never held a hearing or sent it to the floor, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the Federal Living Wage Responsibility Act on March 5, 2009, joined by three original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and the House Education and Labor Committee on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011 [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 8 cosponsors in total, all Democrats, and never had a Senate companion recorded in its action history [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors and the federal government's procurement budget are better off because the bill died: the wage floor, restitution, and five-year debarment penalties never took effect, and low-wage federal contract workers kept their pre-existing pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal contractors and the procurement budget

sides.party_line_note: All 9 supporters (the sponsor and 8 cosponsors) were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored and no vote was ever taken, so opposition is visible only as inaction rather than a recorded bloc.

industries.industry: Federal contractors (janitorial, food service, security, and other service firms)
industries.note: Covered contractors would have to raise pay to the family-of-four poverty line and pay supplements for missing benefits, raising labor costs; repeat violators faced contract cancellation and a five-year ban. Their gain from the bill's death was keeping wages and enforcement where they were.
Agencies would pay higher wages to any full-time employees earning below the poverty line, but would gain clearer rules and restitution powers against scofflaw contractors.
Nonprofits are exempt unless their CEO earns more than 25 times their lowest full-time worker, a carve-out that preserves low pay at organizations below that ratio.
Small-business contractors are entirely exempt, so they would keep competing for federal contracts without the wage obligation their larger rivals faced.
